Musk's SpaceX is still restricting Starlink in Ukraine and the toll is rising
headlines.summary: Since last week, Ukraine has reported restrictions on Starshield, a version of SpaceX's Starlink, hampering its military operations against Russia.
headlines.article_text: Ukraine says Starlink restrictions remain despite Trump assurances Skip Navigation Markets Business Investing Tech Politics & Policy Video Watchlist Investing Club PRO Livestream Menu Key Points Ukrainian officials continued to report issues with SpaceX's Starlink internet system on Friday. National security expert Dmitri Alperovitch said that Ukraine is losing drones and that restrictions are limiting strikes on Russian logistics. Trump, who said Thursday that Elon Musk had "put it back," said Friday that he hadn't spoken with the SpaceX CEO about Ukraine's Starlink service. In this article SPCX Follow your favorite stocks CREATE FREE ACCOUNT watch now VIDEO 1:51 01:51 President Trump: Don’t know who ordered the Starlink slowdown in Ukraine Squawk on the Street SpaceX 's Starlink internet system continues to be throttled in Ukraine as the stakes rise for the war-torn country, Ukrainian officials and a national security expert said Friday. "Every day matters for Ukraine, because every Ukrainian life matters," wrote Denys Sienik, Ukraine's deputy ambassador to the U.S., in a Friday post on X . "Our people are waiting for positive news, hoping that the restrictions will be lifted and our defenders will have the capabilities they need to protect lives," Sienik said. "Unfortunately, as of today, nothing has changed. We continue to wait." Since Oct. 14, Ukrainian officials have accused SpaceX of undermining the country's ability to defend itself by imposing speed limits on Starshield, the military-grade Starlink offering. Any drone traveling above 100 mph lost its connection, disrupting some missions, officials said. Despite recent comments from President Donald Trump that indicated service was restored, Ukraine's Starshield terminals continued to experience problems on Friday, said Dmitri Alperovitch, chairman of the Silverado Policy Accelerator, a Washington, D.C., think tank focused on energy, defense tech and global trade. "They are losing drones," Alperovitch, who is also a co-founder and former chief technology officer of cybersecurity firm CrowdStrike , told CNBC. "Ability to do mid strike to hit Russian logistics is now limited." Soldiers from a separate task rifle battalion of the National Police of Ukraine in the Zaporizhzhia region take a camouflage case off a Starlink satellite communication terminal to be set up at a combat position in the Donetsk region, Ukraine, October 16, 2026. Dmytro Smolienko | Future Publishing | Getty Images Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said in a Friday post on X that the restrictions on Starlink and Starshield "are still there," and added, "The speed has not been restored." He noted that the country is also waiting for the U.S. to deliver missile interceptors "that were already agreed on." "Things have become harder — partly because of the Starlink and Starshield policies and speed limits," Zelenskyy wrote. "But our frontline is still holding and I am proud of how strong our people are." Zelenskyy's defense tech advisor, Serhii Beskrestnov, also confirmed the restrictions were in place in a post on his Telegram channel. "While there are isolated cases where Starlink may operate somewhat beyond the established limits, this is likely a result of SpaceX's algorithms or specific usage conditions, rather than an actual removal of restrictions," Beskrestnov said in a post translated by Google. Elon Musk and representatives from SpaceX did not immediately respond to a request for comment. Who is ultimately responsible for the decision to limit Ukraine's service remains unclear. Democratic lawmakers have since called for an investigation into Musk and the Starshield throttling. A group of bipartisan lawmakers penned a letter to Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth on Thursday urging the agency to "act expeditiously to expand its Starshield arrangements and ensure uninterrupted satellite communications support for Ukraine." The Wall Street Journal reported on Thursday that Trump spoke to Musk by phone about lifting the restrictions on Ukraine's Starshield terminals. Trump said Thursday he didn't "want to comment one way or the other" about whether he made the call to Musk, and added, "The bottom line, he put it back." But on Friday, Trump insisted that he hadn't spoken with Musk, and reiterated that Starshield service had been restored. "I've heard it was fixed," Trump told reporters outside the White House. "But if it's not, I'll speak to him." Amid the Starshield disruptions, Zelenskyy and other Ukrainian officials have floated the possibility of adopting additional satellite internet communications systems. Experts previously told CNBC that it could prove challenging for Ukraine or other countries to secure alternatives to Starlink since other options are not yet comparable to the service. Zelenskyy wrote Wednesday in a post on X that he met with Norwegian officials and Kongsberg, a Norwegian defense company, to discuss air defense systems and "launching work on new satellite communication capabilities for our warriors." On Thursday, Ukraine's Ministry of Defense signed a letter of intent with Nokia and ICEYE, a Finnish space intelligence firm, to "explore cooperation in space" and "support Ukraine's defense capabilities, particularly in building sovereign satellite communications," the companies said in a release. "Modern warfare has proven that reliable communications are a matter of national security," Zelenskyy said in a statement. "We must all rely on capabilities that we can control." -- CNBC's Eamon Javers and Lora Kolodny contributed reporting to this story. headlines.article_text: American Express is cutting 5% of its workforce to 'prepare for AI' Skip Navigation Markets Business Investing Tech Politics & Policy Video Watchlist Investing Club PRO Livestream Menu Key Points American Express is cutting about 5% of its global workforce. Chief Financial Officer Christophe Le Caillec told CNBC in an interview that the restructuring was to make American Express "leaner, more agile, and also to prepare for AI." Amex had almost 77,000 employees at the end of 2025. In this article AXP Follow your favorite stocks CREATE FREE ACCOUNT Stephen Squeri, chairman and chief executive officer of American Express Co., speaks during an Economic Club of New York event in New York, US, on Thursday, Nov. 10, 2022. Stephanie Keith | Bloomberg | Getty Images American Express is cutting thousands of employees as the leading credit card company prepares for artificial intelligence to take over more of its internal processes. Amex is eliminating 5% of its global workforce and taking a $336 million restructuring charge, CEO Stephen Squeri told analysts Friday on the company's third-quarter earnings call. The firm had almost 77,000 employees at the end of 2025. Chief Financial Officer Christophe Le Caillec told CNBC in an interview that the restructuring was to make American Express "leaner, more agile, and also to prepare for AI." "You don't want to automate processes that are not optimally structured," Le Caillec said. "So what we're doing here is to reduce layers and increase spans of controls, so that we can automate and take advantage of AI in the coming quarters and the coming years." The Amex announcement reflects a broader trend across financial services, where banks are working to replace repetitive roles with AI automation. On Thursday, Barclays confirmed plans to trim 5,000 jobs — also roughly 5% of its staff — in another tech-driven cost initiative. The moves come even as the sector is enjoying robust profits from growing consumer spending and resilient credit. During the analyst call, Squeri said the charge was to improve the company's efficiency. "We've got good momentum, but to accelerate innovation and win over the next few years, we needed to become [a] more agile and efficient organization," Squeri said. 'Run rogue' Squeri devoted a 10-minute section of his prepared remarks to his views on AI, focusing mainly on how it will be used to personalize experiences and offers for Amex cardholders. While the CEO emphasized the need to meet customers' desires to use AI, including agents, he added that Amex is "not going to let assistants run rogue through our system." "We need to protect our customers [and] merchants, and we're only going to allow agents to access our systems that are either approved through API or MCP channels," he said, citing two ways to securely connect outside platforms with Amex systems. Amex posted quarterly results that topped Wall Street profit expectations. Adjusted earnings per share were $4.68, beating the $4.48 average estimate of analysts, according to LSEG. The company raised its full-year earnings guidance to a range of $18.30 to $18.60 per share, on an unadjusted basis, up from its previous target of $17.30 to $17.90. That metric was helped by proceeds from Amex's sale of its stake in Global Business Travel Group , part of which went into the restructuring plan, Le Caillec said. Total revenue rose 9% to $20.06 billion, coming in slightly below Wall Street's $20.12 billion LSEG forecast. Executives attributed part of the spending drag to recent exits from small business co-brand partnerships. Shares of the card company fell roughly 4% in afternoon trading. headlines.article_text: Ukraine partners with Nokia and ICEYE for Starlink alternative Skip Navigation Markets Business Investing Tech Politics & Policy Video Watchlist Investing Club PRO Livestream Menu Key Points After SpaceX imposed speed limits on Starlink that hampered Ukraine's military operations, Kyiv is looking for alternatives. Finnish mobile giant Nokia and satellite maker ICEYE signed a letter of intent with Ukraine's Ministry of Defense on Thursday to develop new satellite capabilities. "Modern warfare has proven that reliable communications are a matter of national security," Ukraine President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said in a statement. In this article NOK SPCX Follow your favorite stocks CREATE FREE ACCOUNT A Ukrainian uses a Starlink satellite-internet communication system on a rooftop in Kyiv, Ukraine, March 11, 2025. Andrew Kravchenko | Bloomberg | Getty Images After SpaceX restricted use of its Starlink and Starshield satellite internet services in Ukraine, causing fast-moving drones to disconnect and drop out of the sky, Kyiv is looking for alternatives. Ukraine's Ministry of Defense said on Thursday that it has signed a letter of intent to develop new defense and satellite communication capabilities in partnership with Finnish tech companies Nokia and ICEYE, which makes satellites. "Modern warfare has proven that reliable communications are a matter of national security," Ukraine President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said in a statement . "We must all rely on capabilities that we can control." Zelenskyy also announced a partnership with Norway this week to jointly develop air defense and communications systems that could serve as an alternative to Starshield. As of Friday, Ukraine officials said the country is still experiencing restrictions on Starlink, which cut connectivity for drones or other aircraft that travel at speeds over 100 miles per hour. Both the Trump administration and SpaceX CEO Elon Musk have shirked responsibility for unannounced Starlink service changes that Ukraine reported more than a week ago. President Donald Trump told reporters at the White House on Friday that he would call on Musk to lift the restrictions. SpaceX executives didn't respond to a request for comment. Lawmakers in the U.S. from both parties are calling for a formal probe of Musk and SpaceX regarding the alleged unilateral changes the company made to its services in Ukraine. Jay Shambaugh, a senior fellow at Brookings and professor of economics and international affairs at George Washington University, told CNBC in an email the sudden Starlink changes are "part of a pattern since Trump came back into office of the United States acting as an unreliable ally." Shambaugh cautioned that, "over time, that can reduce U.S. exports to the EU if those countries don't want to be dependent on something where the U.S. can cut them off." Rivals to Starlink are on the horizon, including Amazon's Leo , France's Eutelsat , and a forthcoming service from Jeff Bezos' Blue Origin called TeraWave , which has yet to deploy its first satellites. Beyond Ukraine, several countries are looking into sovereign satellite communications systems. The EU is building IRIS² , a constellation of hundreds of satellites, but its first launches aren't expected until 2029. Since Russia's invasion of Ukraine in February 2022, venture and private equity investors have poured about $8 billion into Starlink and Starshield alternatives, according to research by Chad Anderson, CEO of Space Capital, which tracks industry deals. About $3.9 billion of that funding has gone to potential Starlink competitors, mostly Spacesail and China SatNet. Virginia Burger, senior defense policy analyst with the Project on Government Oversight, told CNBC in an interview that the problem today is there's no drop-in replacement for Starlink, and combat is moving more into "unmanned systems, drone warfare and other systems that require high-speed internet." -- CNBC's Annie Palmer contributed reporting. Beneath the chaos surrounding Moderna and Merck 's latest data on their personalized cancer vaccine, oncologists see something else: an important milestone in melanoma treatment. The companies on Thursday released detailed results from a phase 3 trial on their mRNA-based shot after partial data leaked on social media platforms earlier that day. The vaccine, known as intismeran autogene, reduced the risk of melanoma recurrence or death by 42% when given alongside Merck's immunotherapy Keytruda, compared with Keytruda alone. The combination also reduced the risk of cancer spreading to distant parts of the body or death by 38%, compared with just the immunotherapy, according to the trial on roughly 1,100 patients whose tumors were removed by surgery. The stock market's reaction contrasted with the assessment of six melanoma specialists, who told CNBC the results represent a clinically meaningful advance that could eventually become a standard of care for patients who undergo surgery first and have not received immunotherapy before their operation. watch now VIDEO 3:50 03:50 Merck CEO on melanoma vaccine results: The prescribing community will find results quite meaningful Squawk on the Street "This has the potential to be a major breakthrough in melanoma treatment and also cancer immunotherapy in general that will open the door to greater outcomes for patients," said Dr. Sekwon Jang, a melanoma specialist at Inova Schar Cancer and principal investigator at one of the trial's U.S. sites. Dr. Janice Mehnert, NYU Langone skin cancer specialist and trial investigator, added that "this is the first time we're seeing that when you add something to immunotherapy, you actually boost the efficacy of the immunotherapy." The vaccine is not far from potentially entering the market for the first time and reaching melanoma patients. In an interview ahead of the results, Moderna CEO Stéphane Bancel said the company is finishing a filing with regulators as it aims to get the drug fully approved next year. "It's a very, very happy moment for the field, for patients," he said. Major advance in melanoma An immunotherapy like Keytruda wakes up the immune system to detect and attack cancer cells. Unlike preventative vaccines, which protect against infections that can cause cancer, Moderna and Merck's treatment acts like a blueprint to train the immune system to recognize and hunt residual cancer cells based on the specific mutations in an individual patient's tumor. The significance of the phase 3 data extends beyond delaying a recurrence, doctors said. Melanoma can become much more difficult to treat when it returns after surgery and spreads to distant parts of the body, such as the lungs, brain or liver. Patients with advanced disease may require additional treatments, including immunotherapy, radiation or further surgery, and those methods are not guaranteed to work. Preventing the cancer from returning could spare patients from ever facing the risks and complexities of metastatic disease altogether. "If we can essentially cure more patients with earlier-stage melanoma and never have to deal with unresectable metastatic disease — that's a wonderful advance," said Dr. Michael Postow, chief of the Melanoma Service at Memorial Sloan Kettering Cancer Center and an investigator on the trial. Ideally, patients in the future may be able to undergo surgery and receive the vaccine and Keytruda without needing further melanoma treatment, Postow told CNBC. Still, questions remain about whether the combination ultimately helps patients live longer, what the benefit looks like over longer periods of time and which patients benefit most. The results also leave open where the personalized vaccine would fit into a changing melanoma treatment landscape, some experts said. The trial tested the vaccine after surgery, alongside Keytruda, rather than against immunotherapy regimens given before surgery. That's an approach increasingly used for eligible patients with resectable melanoma, where the primary tumor can be removed. The data does not show that using the vaccine approach is more or less effective than receiving immunotherapy before surgery. The medical community will get more clarity after Moderna and Merck present the detailed results at the European Society for Medical Oncology conference on Saturday. Investors diverged from doctors Moderna shares fell as much as 25% Thursday, before regaining some ground, after partial data from the trial leaked on social media. The sell-off came despite the positive results, underscoring the gap between the treatment's clinical promise and investor expectations for its commercial potential. Moderna shares are also up nearly 600% this year due to the cancer shot optimism, creating more potential for a Wall Street letdown. Investors had hoped the vaccine and Keytruda would replicate the results of an earlier phase 2 trial, which showed a roughly 49% reduction in the risk of recurrence or death at five years, RBC Capital Markets analyst Trung Huynh wrote in a note Thursday. Huynh described the phase 3 results as clinically meaningful and likely to support regulatory approval, but said the primary efficacy result landed at the low end of investor expectations. But there was a key difference in the studies: The phase 3 trial included patients with a broader range of risk profiles, including some at lower risk of recurrence than those enrolled in the earlier phase 2 trial, said Dr. George Ansstas, who leads the melanoma department at Washington University in St. Louis. That may have slightly tempered the results, since patients considered lower risk have less chance of recurrence to begin with. "It's great data actually. It's overall consistent with what we've proven in the phase 2 trial," said Ansstas, who also worked on the phase 2 trial. The combination showed little difference from Keytruda alone during the first six months of treatment, the companies said. But a separate analysis of the phase 3 data offered a more encouraging signal about the treatment's effect after the six-month mark. The vaccine and Keytruda reduced the risk of recurrence or death by 58% after that point, compared with Keytruda alone. The 42% figure comes from the primary analysis, which included patients' outcomes throughout the trial's follow-up period. The median follow-up was about two years at the time of the analysis, so the result reflects the overall treatment effect, not just what happened before or after the six-month mark. Ansstas said the benefit of the personalized cancer vaccine may take several months to emerge because each shot must be custom-manufactured, a process that can take roughly six weeks, while patients begin Keytruda in the meantime. After vaccination begins, the immune system also needs time and repeated doses to develop a response against tumors. That timeline could help explain why the group that received the combination regimen saw even greater benefits around six months, Ansstas said.
